extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, and practicing school mathematics teachers interested in supporting classroom argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and teacher knowledge (MKT) needed to support students' development of valid mathematical arguments in collaborative classroom problem solving; includes identifying and responding to students' arguments, using representations and counterexamples, and designing interventions. Based on video case study with elementary teachers and students working on combinatorics 'tower' tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: SCK – knowledge of argumentation as a mathematical process
rubrics_metrics.description: SCK – knowledge of argumentation as a mathematical process, including its components, structure, and function (e.g., Toulmin’s scheme, types of arguments, valid and invalid argument and functions and roles of arguments)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats understanding of argument structure (claims, data, warrants, backing, qualifiers, rebuttals) as subject-specific knowledge that helps teachers identify validity/invalidity of student arguments (examples: recognizing duplicate data in Martina's towers; identifying implicit warrants such as 'height x height'). May be used to analyze and critique students' reasoning and to design appropriate challenges or supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: KCS – knowledge of content and students’ thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: KCS - knowledge of students’ typical conceptions and misconceptions as well as what they can do when engaging in argumentation (e.g., typical Harel and Sowder’s (2007) proof schemes that student may use to determine if an argument is convincing or not)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes anticipating common student argumentative strategies (e.g., 'height x height' generalization, reasoning-by-cases, diagonal strategy) so teachers can design targeted interventions or counterexamples; informs interpretation of students' representations and expectations about how their reasoning will unfold (example: the researcher's anticipation of students predicting 'nine' for 3-tall towers).

rubrics_metrics.name: KCT – knowledge of content and teaching: eliciting and responding interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: KCT – Knowledge of interventions for (1) eliciting and (2) responding to students’ arguments (e.g., how to help students transition from authoritarian or empirical justification toward more analytical types of arguments; how to challenge invalid arguments; how to support generalization of arguments)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers practical teacher moves: prompting students to establish claims and justifications, asking guiding questions ('How do you know?'), involving peers in critique, supplying or pointing out omitted data/warrants/backing, modeling argument construction and confrontation, and designing tasks (e.g., counterexample tasks) that elicit deeper justification. Examples: teacher removing duplicates and soliciting peer agreement in Martina episode; researcher-suggested task sequence to expose invalid 'height x height' warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentation as a discursive/social practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A view of argumentation that emphasizes social and cultural aspects and persuasion as the main function of the process (as opposed to solely structural/cognitive validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should treat argumentation as collective/discursive activity: negotiate classroom norms, involve peers in evaluating arguments, and leverage collaborative interaction to make functions of statements (data, warrants, backing) negotiable. Example: teacher used other students' interventions to help Martina see duplicates; social interaction produced the resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counterexamples to challenge invalid warrants
rubrics_metrics.description: Using counterexamples (carefully chosen tasks) to challenge general warrants implicit in students' arguments (e.g., the 3-tall towers task as a counterexample to the 'height x height' warrant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should design or prompt empirical investigations/prediction-then-test activities so students encounter disequilibrium when a general warrant fails; counterexamples can reveal that an implicit warrant is not valid and so help students abandon or revise invalid generalizations (example: students predicted nine for 3-tall towers but found eight, leading to questioning of the 3x3 warrant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of students’ typical argumentative strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of the argumentative strategies students are likely to use (e.g., proof-by-cases, diagonal strategy, 'height x height' heuristic) and how these strategies manifest in tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge enables teachers to anticipate reasoning moves, notice productive ideas, and choose interventions that build on students' strategies. Lack of familiarity can constrain teacher support (example: T5 did not recognize the diagonal strategy with three colors and so missed an opportunity to support Yonny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attending to and using representations of mathematical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers' attention to students’ external representations (e.g., tower arrangements, diagonals, groupings) as evidentiary artifacts that reveal emerging argument structure and strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations can expose cases/groups and proof structure; teachers should examine, question, and prompt reorganization of representations to make implicit warrants/covering cases explicit. Example: teacher's attention to Yonny's arrangement revealed missing diagonals/opposite-group organization and enabled a teacher-led prompt that produced an 'aha' and a complete proof-by-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging abductive forms of reasoning via empirical investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies for countering abductive or model-based explanations (students giving explanations that describe the models they built) by provoking empirical tests of general warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abductive arguments often appear convincing because the constructed model supports the claim; teachers can challenge them by asking students to test whether the general warrant holds across related cases, thereby creating cognitive disequilibrium and prompting revision (example: using three-tall and five-tall variations to show 'height x height' fails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to analyze arguments using Toulmin’s scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Toulmin’s argumentation model (claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal) as an analytical tool for classroom arguments, both individual and collective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers and researchers can code and interpret student utterances and interactions with this model to identify missing/implicit elements (e.g., implicit warrants), to plan interventions, and to recognize when collective argumentation negotiates roles of statements. The paper uses Toulmin coding in video analyses (example: Martina's argument coded with data, implicit warrant, invalid claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific teacher intervention moves for supporting argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete discursive moves teachers can use: prompt students to establish claims and justifications, ask peers to evaluate and agree/disagree, remove or highlight incorrect data, ask guiding questions ('What happens if...?','Do you agree?','How do you know?'), model construction and confrontation of arguments, and organize whole-class sharing of written solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective moves often combine SCK, KCS, and KCT: (1) identify structural issue (SCK), (2) draw on knowledge of likely student strategies (KCS), and (3) select an eliciting or responding move (KCT). Anti-patterns include assuming little scaffolding is needed, failing to draw peers into evaluation, or walking away when a student's warrant is unexamined (example: teacher walked away from Gabe's 4x4 explanation without eliciting the convincing argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promoting equity via argumentation opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing all students with opportunities to produce and defend their arguments in classroom discussions to promote equitable access to mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentation as discourse influences access; teachers should negotiate norms and structure discussions so that diverse students can present and critique arguments. This is noted as a rationale for promoting argumentation (references to NCTM, CCSSM) and connects to teacher moves that ensure inclusive participation.
